narrative:
Your law school application was denied because our model predicted a 54 percent chance that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. That means the risk of failing was slightly larger than the chance of passing, and the admissions committee decided not to accept that risk.

The strongest factor in the model’s decision was your class decile in the third year of your undergraduate program. This actually worked in your favor: being in the fifth decile pushed the prediction toward passing the bar, even though it was slightly below the average decile of students who were accepted (around 5.8). So your junior-year grades were a positive signal.

However, your LSAT score had almost as much influence, and it moved strongly in the opposite direction. At 23, your score was far below the average of 37 among accepted applicants. This one score alone substantially increased the predicted chance of failure. Your undergraduate GPA also contributed meaningfully to the denial. At 2.30, it fell well short of the 3.23 average for admitted students, adding another significant push toward the “fail” outcome.

In short, while your third-year class standing suggested you could succeed academically, the combination of a very low LSAT score and a low undergraduate GPA outweighed that positive sign. The model saw these two weaknesses as strong indicators that you might struggle on the bar exam.

To improve your chances in the future, focus on raising your LSAT score through dedicated preparation and consider retaking the exam. You might also strengthen your academic record by completing additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program. Because the prediction was close, improving even one of these areas could shift the outcome in your favor.
